text:
The crash happens because the app requests `POST_NOTIFICATIONS` on Android 14 and then assumes the user granted it, so when someone taps Deny the callback reads a null channel and throws. Older Android versions never showed that dialog, which is why the bug only appeared after the target SDK moved to 34.

The fix is small. Check the grant result before you touch the channel, and fall back to a silent in-app banner when the permission is missing. I would also add an instrumented test that denies the permission, because the emulator image for API 34 makes that easy to script.

The fix is small. Check the grant result first. Then touch the channel. Fall back to a silent in-app banner. Add an instrumented test that denies the permission. The API 34 emulator image makes that easy.

topic: slow docker build on apple silicon
text:
Your build takes about 14 minutes on the M3 machines because the base image is `linux/amd64` only, so Docker runs every `RUN` step under QEMU emulation. The CI runners are x86, which is why nobody noticed the slowdown there.

Switching to the multi-arch tag of the same base image should bring the local build down to roughly 3 minutes. If you need an amd64 artifact on a Mac, build it with `docker buildx build` and the platform set to `linux/amd64`, but only for the final release step, and keep everyday builds native. The cache mount for `pip` also helps, but it matters much less than removing emulation.

The gaps in the latency panel line up with the Prometheus scrape interval, which you raised to 60 seconds last week while the panel still uses a `rate()` window of 30 seconds. When the window is shorter than two scrapes, `rate()` has fewer than two samples and returns nothing, so Grafana draws a hole.

Set the window to `$__rate_interval` instead of a fixed value, and Grafana will pick a range that always covers enough samples. The data itself is complete, so you do not need to backfill anything.

topic: flaky dns lookup in a container
text:
The lookups fail about one time in twenty because the container inherits `ndots:5` from the Kubernetes default, so a short name like `billing` gets tried against four search domains before the real one. Each attempt sends an A and an AAAA query in parallel over the same UDP socket, and the conntrack race in the node kernel occasionally drops one of them, which leaves the resolver waiting for its 5 second timeout.

Setting `single-request-reopen` in the pod `dnsConfig` avoids the race. Using fully qualified names with a trailing dot also cuts the number of queries, and together the two changes removed the timeouts in my test run of 10,000 lookups.

topic: flaky dns lookup in a container
text:
The lookups fail about one time in twenty. The container inherits `ndots:5`. A short name like `billing` hits four search domains first. Each attempt sends an A query. It also sends an AAAA query. Both share one UDP socket. The node kernel has a conntrack race. It drops one query. The resolver waits 5 seconds.

Set `single-request-reopen` in the pod `dnsConfig`. That avoids the race. Use fully qualified names with a trailing dot. That cuts the queries. I ran 10,000 lookups. The timeouts were gone.

The proposed `/orders` endpoint uses `page` and `per_page`, which works for the admin table but breaks for the sync client, because new orders arrive while it pages and shift every later page by a few rows. That client will skip or repeat orders, and nobody will see it until a reconciliation report disagrees.

I would offer cursor pagination for the sync use case. Return an opaque `next_cursor` built from `created_at` and `id`, and keep offset paging only where humans jump to page 7. The response should also include a hard cap of 200 items, so that a single request cannot pull the whole table.

Offer cursor pagination for sync. Return an opaque `next_cursor`. Build it from `created_at` and `id`. Keep offset paging for the admin table. Humans jump to page 7 there. Cap responses at 200 items. One request cannot pull the whole table then.

The client reconnects every 200 ms because the server closes the socket with code 1008 after the token expires, and the reconnect handler treats every close code the same way. It opens a new socket with the same expired token, the server rejects it, and the loop runs until the tab is closed. We saw 40,000 connection attempts from a single browser on 3 March.

The handler should refresh the token when it sees 1008 and back off exponentially for other codes, starting at one second and capping at 30. Add jitter as well, so that a server restart does not bring every client back in the same second.

The client reconnects every 200 ms. The token expires. The server closes the socket with code 1008. The handler ignores the code. It opens a new socket. It sends the same expired token. The server rejects it. The loop repeats. We saw 40,000 attempts from one browser on 3 March.

First, refresh the token on 1008. Then back off exponentially for other codes. Start at one second. Cap at 30. Add jitter. A server restart will not sync every client then.

The session keys disappeared because the instance runs with `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`, so when the new rate limiter filled memory to the 4 GB limit, Redis evicted the least recently used keys regardless of their TTL. Sessions of users who had been idle for an hour were the oldest entries, which is why those users were logged out first.

Move the rate limiter to its own instance, or switch this one to `volatile-lru` and make sure sessions are the only keys without a TTL. I would also add an alert on `evicted_keys`, because the counter rose from zero to 180,000 on Tuesday and nobody was watching it.

The instance runs `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru`. The new rate limiter filled memory. It hit the 4 GB limit. Redis evicted the least recently used keys. It ignored TTLs. Idle sessions were the oldest entries. They went first. Those users were logged out.

Move the rate limiter to its own instance. Or switch this one to `volatile-lru`. Then sessions must be the only keys without a TTL. Add an alert on `evicted_keys`. The counter rose from zero on Tuesday. It reached 180,000. Nobody was watching it.

Pushes started failing on Monday because the organization used up its 50 GB of Git LFS bandwidth, and most of that came from the CI job that clones the design repo with full LFS checkout on every pipeline run. The job only needs two font files, but it downloads 1.2 GB of PSD exports each time.

Set `GIT_LFS_SKIP_SMUDGE=1` in that job and pull only the fonts with an include pattern on `git lfs pull`, which should cut usage by more than 90 percent. Buying another data pack would unblock pushes today, although without the CI change it would run out again in about a week.

The kernel dies at cell 14 because `pd.read_csv` loads the full 9 GB event log into memory, and the `merge` that follows makes a second copy before the first one is released. On a 16 GB laptop that leaves nothing for the browser, so the OS kills the kernel without a Python traceback.

Read only the six columns you use, set `dtype` for the ID columns, and the frame shrinks to about 2 GB. If you need every row, process the file in chunks of a million and aggregate as you go, which keeps peak memory flat no matter how large the log grows.

The build broke after the bump to ESLint 9 because version 9 ignores `.eslintrc.json` and looks for `eslint.config.js`, so the CI step found no config and failed with a message that reads like a missing plugin. topic: accessibility issue with a modal dialog
text:
When the delete confirmation opens, focus stays on the button underneath, so a screen reader user hears nothing and keeps tabbing through the page behind the overlay. They cannot find the dialog. Sighted keyboard users have a milder version of the same problem, since the focus ring sits behind a dimmed backdrop where nobody can see it.

Move focus to the dialog heading when it opens, trap it inside until the user confirms or cancels, and return it to the trigger afterwards. Using the native `dialog` element with `showModal()` gives you most of that behavior for free.

topic: security scan finding in a base image
text:
The scanner flags a critical OpenSSL CVE in our base image, and the report makes it look like every service is exposed. Most are not. The vulnerable function is only reachable when a process parses untrusted certificates, which in our stack happens in the ingress proxy and nowhere else.

That still means we patch, and the updated base image from the vendor has been available since Friday. I would rebuild the proxy today and let the other services pick up the new base with their next regular release, instead of forcing thirty redeploys at once.

text:
These are the retention settings currently live in production.

topic: summary of a customer support ticket trend
text:
Ticket volume for September came in at 4,120, about 9 percent above August.

Billing questions are the largest group. Password resets dropped after the magic link launch. The mobile app accounts for a third of new tickets. First response time is 2.4 hours on average. Satisfaction held at 91 percent.

The one new pattern is a cluster of complaints about duplicate charges, which I traced to a retry bug in the payment webhook.

Rotate the key in this order so that nothing breaks in between:

1. Create a new key in the provider dashboard.
2. Add it to the secret store as `PAYMENTS_KEY_NEXT`.
3. Deploy the services that read the new name.
4. Confirm in the logs that requests succeed.
5. Revoke the old key.
6. Delete the old secret.

The whole sequence takes about twenty minutes if the deploy pipeline is quiet.

topic: estimate for a migration to a new payment provider
text:
My estimate is six to eight weeks. Most of that time does not go into the API integration itself, which is two weeks of work for one developer, but into migrating stored cards, because the new provider can only import them through a PCI compliant transfer that both vendors have to schedule and that usually takes three to four weeks to arrange.

We can run the two providers side by side during that period, sending new customers to the new one while existing subscriptions keep billing through the old one until their cards have moved.

Die Clients haben daraufhin sofort einen weiteren Versuch gestartet, was die Schleife bis etwa 14:52 am Laufen hielt.

Der Reconnect braucht einen exponentiellen Backoff mit Zufallsanteil, der bei einer Sekunde beginnt und bei 30 Sekunden endet. Außerdem sollten wir die Pods beim Rollout schrittweise ersetzen, damit nie alle Verbindungen auf einmal abreißen.

Der Build dauert lokal 18 Minuten, weil die `COPY . .`-Anweisung vor `npm ci` steht und damit jede Änderung an einer beliebigen Datei den Cache für die Abhängigkeiten ungültig macht. Dazu kommt, dass `node_modules` nicht in der `.dockerignore` steht, sodass Docker bei jedem Build rund 900 MB an den Daemon schickt.

Kopiert zuerst nur `package.json` und `package-lock.json`, führt dann `npm ci` aus und kopiert erst danach den restlichen Code. Mit dem ergänzten `.dockerignore` lag ein Build ohne neue Abhängigkeiten in meinem Test bei 70 Sekunden.

So stellt ihr die DNS-Timeouts lokal nach:

1. Startet den Container mit `docker compose up resolver-test`.
2. Öffnet eine Shell im Container.
3. Führt `./lookup-loop.sh billing 1000` aus.
4. Zählt die Zeilen mit `timeout` im Log.

Bei mir lag die Fehlerquote vor der Änderung bei etwa fünf Prozent und danach bei null.

Falls der neue Checkout Probleme macht, geht ihr so vor:

1. Öffnet das Admin-Panel.
2. Setzt `checkout_v2` auf null Prozent.
3. Prüft im Dashboard, ob die Fehlerrate sinkt.
4. Schreibt eine kurze Meldung in den Incident-Kanal.
5. Informiert das Checkout-Team.

Der Entwurf ist gut. Für die Admin-Tabelle passt die Paginierung mit `page` und `per_page`, weil dort Menschen gezielt auf eine bestimmte Seite springen wollen, aber der Sync-Client sollte einen Cursor bekommen, da sich die Seiten sonst verschieben, sobald während des Abrufs neue Bestellungen eingehen, und der Client dann Einträge doppelt verarbeitet oder überspringt.

Das hat uns überrascht. Wir sollten die geplante DATEV-Anbindung deshalb vorziehen und im nächsten Quartal messen, ob die Kündigungen in dieser Gruppe tatsächlich zurückgehen.
